title: Bread in the Wilderness, a Path through the Sea
sum: Herod Antipas hears about Jesus and fears that John the Baptist, whom he beheaded, has come back to life. Matthew tells the story of John's death in flashback: John had condemned Herod's marriage to his brother's wife Herodias, and at Herod's birthday feast her daughter danced, Herod swore a rash oath, and John's head was brought in on a platter.

Jesus withdraws to a lonely place, but the crowds follow. Moved with pity, he heals them, then feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, with five loaves and two fish; twelve baskets are left over. That night he walks on the sea to his disciples, who are struggling against the wind. Peter walks toward him, sinks and is rescued, and the disciples worship Jesus as God's Son. At Gennesaret the sick are healed by touching the tassel of his cloak.
readings: Read as history

The account of John's death agrees in substance with Josephus, who says Antipas killed John at Machaerus, though for political reasons. The feeding is the only miracle told in all four Gospels, and many historians accept that Jesus held a large meal in the wilderness that his followers remembered as a sign. The walking on the sea is beyond historical proof either way; believers take it as a miracle, and others as a resurrection-style vision or a symbolic story.
Read as a story built on Scripture

The chapter retells Israel's exodus: bread in the wilderness, like the manna, and a path through the sea, like the crossing of the Red Sea. Jesus does what the Old Testament says only God does: he feeds his people, "tramples on the back of the Sea" (Job 9:8) and says "I am." Peter's sinking and rescue picture the church in danger, saved by the Lord's hand.

views.H: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39 as a tetrarch, not a king. His marriage to Herodias, the wife of a half-brother, provoked a war with the Nabatean king whose daughter he divorced. Josephus places John's execution at Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. The feeding probably took place near Bethsaida on the northeast shore (Luke 9:10). Galilean fishing boats, like the one found between Ginosar and Magdala in 1986, held about a dozen people.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 6:14–56 closely but shortens it: Herod wants to kill John rather than protect him (compare Mark 6:20), and the disciples worship Jesus instead of failing to understand (compare Mark 6:52). The story of Peter on the water is found only in Matthew. Many scholars see in the two feedings and the sea crossing a deliberate pattern drawn from Exodus and from the Elisha stories (2 Kings 4:42–44).
views.L: Two banquets stand side by side: Herod's birthday feast, ending in death, and Jesus' meal in the wilderness, giving life. Peter's sinking is a small drama of faith and doubt; Jesus' words "You with so little faith, why did you waver?" sum it up. The chapter moves from the question "Who is this?" (14:2) to the confession "You really are God's Son" (14:33).
views.J: The feeding recalls the manna and Elisha's miracle of loaves, and the twelve baskets suggest the twelve tribes. Many Jews hoped that the Messiah would bring back the manna. The blessing over bread follows the Jewish table blessing to God "who brings forth bread from the earth." The tassel is the fringe commanded in Numbers 15:38, which observant Jews still wear.
views.T: The fathers read the feeding as a sign of the Eucharist: Jesus takes, blesses, breaks and gives, the actions of the Last Supper (26:26). The boat on the stormy sea became the classic image of the church, and Peter's cry "Lord, save me!" a model prayer. Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor John the Baptist's death as a martyrdom, kept on 29 August.

deep.b:
Matthew sets two meals side by side. At Herod's palace, among the powerful, a girl dances, a ruler makes a reckless oath to save face, and a prophet's head comes in on a platter like another dish. In the wilderness, among the sick and the poor, Jesus takes a little bread, gives thanks, and everyone eats until full. One king feeds his guests and kills a prophet; the other king feeds the hungry and heals them.

The contrast belongs to a larger theme. John's death foreshadows Jesus' death: both are prophets, both are held by a ruler who fears the crowd (14:5; 21:46), and both are executed by rulers who seem reluctant (14:9; 27:24). After John's burial his disciples "went to Jesus" (14:12), and Jesus' disciples will one day lay him in a tomb too (27:57–61).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the Rock that sank
deep.b: Matthew uses an unusual verb for Peter's sinking, katapontizomai, "to sink in the deep." In the Greek of Exodus 15:4 it is the very verb for Pharaoh's officers drowned in the Red Sea, and the next verse says they "went down to the bottom like a stone" (Exodus 15:5). In Matthew it occurs once more, at 18:6, where anyone who trips up a little one would be better off "sunk in the open sea." My suggestion: Matthew wants readers to remember, when Jesus later calls Simon "Peter," the rock (16:18), that this rock once sank like Pharaoh's stone-heavy army and was held up only by Jesus' hand. And the leader who sank and was rescued is later told how to treat little ones who stumble (18:6, 12–14). Commentators often note the Rock pun; I have not seen the Exodus link or the link to 18:6 developed in print. This is a guess about Matthew's word choice. The verb is not rare in Greek generally, though its use in the Song of the Sea makes the echo more likely than chance.

echoes: Leviticus 18:16; Leviticus 20:21; Exodus 16:1–36; Numbers 11:13; 2 Kings 4:42–44; Psalm 23:1–2; Exodus 14:21–31; Job 9:8; Job 38:16; Psalm 77:19; Psalm 107:23–30; Isaiah 43:1–3; Isaiah 43:10; Numbers 15:38–40; Mark 6:14–56; Luke 9:7–17; John 6:1–21

settings.what: Herod's verdict on Jesus
settings.to: His court servants, the officials around him
settings.when: When reports of Jesus' work reach the court, some time after John's execution
settings.why: Not to teach but to voice his fear. Herod explains Jesus' powers as John come back from the dead: a guilty conscience reads the new prophet as the old one returned to accuse him.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers would see that even the ruler who killed John could not get rid of God's messengers, and would note the irony: Herod speaks of one "raised from the dead" before Jesus' own resurrection.

settings.what: John's rebuke of Herod
settings.to: Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea
settings.when: Before his arrest, perhaps repeated ("had kept telling him"), around AD 28–29
settings.why: To call a Jewish ruler back to the law of Moses. Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21 forbid marrying a brother's wife while the brother lives, and Herodias had left Herod's half-brother to marry him. John treats Antipas as bound by Israel's law like anyone else.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers saw a prophet who told a ruler the truth and paid for it, a pattern Jesus would follow and his followers might face (10:17–18).
views: Most readers take John's words as a prophet's protest against an unlawful marriage.

Josephus says Antipas feared John's influence over the crowds could lead to revolt. A public charge that the ruler broke God's law could stir exactly that, so the two accounts may describe the same danger from two sides.

settings.what: Jesus' command to feed the crowd
settings.to: The disciples, who want him to send the crowds away
settings.when: Toward evening in a remote place by the lake, after a day of healing
settings.why: To make the disciples share in his work: "Feed them yourselves." What they have seems hopelessly small, but in his hands it is enough. The command anticipates their role as those who hand out bread to the crowds.
settings.readers: For Matthew's church, gathered at the Lord's table, Jesus' words and actions (took, blessed, broke, gave) would sound like their own worship, and the command to feed others like their own mission.

settings.what: The words on the water
settings.to: The frightened disciples in the boat, then Peter alone
settings.when: Between 3 and 6 in the morning, in a headwind, far out on the lake
settings.why: To end their fear by making himself known: "Courage! I am." The phrase is ordinary Greek for "It's me," but it is also how God names himself in the Greek of Isaiah ("I am"). Peter's request and Jesus' "Come" test that word, and Jesus' rescue and rebuke teach that doubt, not the wind, is the real danger.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, a small church in a hostile world, would see themselves in the boat "tormented" by the waves, and hear the risen Lord's promise that he comes to them and holds them up.
views: Traditional readers take the story as an event the disciples witnessed.
A story of faith for the church
Many scholars think Matthew added Peter's walk (it is not in Mark or John) as a teaching scene about faith and doubt, perhaps shaped by Easter appearances.

title: What Makes a Person Unclean
sum: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem ask why Jesus' disciples do not wash their hands before eating, as the tradition of the elders requires. Jesus answers with a charge of his own: their tradition about vows lets a man avoid supporting his parents, against God's command, and he quotes Isaiah on worship from the lips only. To the crowd he says that what goes into the mouth does not make a person unclean, but what comes out of the heart: evil plans, murder, adultery, theft, lies and slander.

In the region of Tyre and Sidon, a Canaanite woman begs Jesus to heal her daughter. He is silent, then says he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel and that the children's bread should not go to the little dogs. She answers that even the little dogs eat the scraps, and Jesus praises her great faith and heals her daughter. Back by the Sea of Galilee he heals many on a mountain, and the crowds praise the God of Israel. He then feeds four thousand men, besides women and children, with seven loaves and a few fish.
readings: Read as a debate within Judaism

Jesus argues like a Jewish teacher: he sets the written law (honor your parents) above an oral rule, and he ranks moral purity above ritual purity, as the prophets did. On this reading he does not abolish the food laws; the dispute is about hand-washing, as 15:20 says, and Matthew's Jewish-Christian church may still have kept kosher.
Read as the opening of the church to the nations

The chapter moves from a dispute about purity, which separated Jews from Gentiles, to a Gentile woman's faith and a meal for crowds that "gave glory to the God of Israel," perhaps Gentiles from the Decapolis. Read this way, the chapter shows the barriers between Israel and the nations beginning to fall, as they do fully in 28:19.

views.H: Hand-washing before ordinary meals was a Pharisaic practice, not a law of Moses; the Mishnah later devotes a whole tractate to it (Yadayim). The korban vow, which set property aside for God, is attested on an ossuary inscription from Jerusalem and discussed in Mishnah Nedarim, where later rabbis allow such vows to be undone for the sake of parents. Tyre and Sidon were wealthy Gentile cities whose territory bordered Galilee and bought its grain.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 7:1–8:10 but leaves out Mark's comment that Jesus "declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19) and ends with hand-washing (15:20). Many scholars conclude that Matthew's church still kept the food laws. In Mark the woman is a "Syrophoenician"; Matthew calls her a "Canaanite," the old enemy of Israel, and adds Jesus' saying about being sent only to Israel (15:24; compare 10:6).
views.L: The chapter is built in pairs: inside and outside, lips and heart, Israel's leaders who take offense and a Gentile woman who has great faith, the children's bread and the little dogs' crumbs. The woman wins an argument with Jesus by taking his own words and turning them, the only person in Matthew to do so.
views.J: Jewish readers will notice that Jesus' opponents defend the oral tradition, which later became the Mishnah and Talmud, and that Jesus himself appeals to Torah. Later rabbis agreed with Jesus that vows must not override duties to parents. The criticism of "blind guides" belongs to a bitter dispute within first-century Judaism and should not be read as a description of Judaism as a whole.
views.T: Christians have usually read 15:11 as freeing believers from the food laws (compare Acts 10; Romans 14:14). The Canaanite woman became a model of humble, persistent prayer; her words lie behind the Anglican Prayer of Humble Access ("We are not worthy so much as to gather up the crumbs under thy table"). Orthodox churches read her story on a Sunday before Lent.

deep.h: Did Jesus cancel the food laws?
deep.b:
Mark, telling the same scene, adds that Jesus "declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19). Matthew does not. He ends the scene with the case in dispute: "Eating without washing your hands does not make anyone unclean" (15:20). Readers differ on what this means.

He set them aside. Most Christians, following Mark, Acts 10 and Romans 14:14, read 15:11 as a principle that ended the food laws for Jesus' followers. He ranked them, without abolishing them. Many scholars, including Jewish scholars such as Geza Vermes, read the saying as a Semitic "not this but that," meaning "not so much this as that": moral impurity matters more than food. Matthew's Jesus says he came not to abolish the law (5:17–19), and his church likely kept kosher. A middle view holds that Matthew believed the food laws still bound Jewish believers but were not required of Gentiles, much as Acts 15 decides.

Either way, the chapter is a dispute about tradition, about whether human rules may override God's command and whether the heart matters more than ritual.

echoes: Exodus 20:12; Exodus 21:17; Leviticus 20:9; Deuteronomy 5:16; Isaiah 29:13; Isaiah 60:21; Isaiah 35:5–6; Isaiah 25:6; Psalm 1:3; Leviticus 11; 1 Kings 17:8–24; Ezekiel 34:16; 2 Kings 4:42–44; Mark 7:1–8:10; Acts 10:9–16; Romans 14:14

settings.what: Jesus' answer about tradition
settings.to: Pharisees and scribes who have come from Jerusalem to question him
settings.when: In Galilee, after the healings at Gennesaret
settings.why: To turn the question around. They ask why his disciples break a tradition; he asks why they break God's command. The korban case shows a human rule (a vow to God) allowed to cancel a written commandment (honor parents). Isaiah's words then name the deeper fault: lip-service without the heart.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, in conflict with the synagogue leaders of their own day, learned to weigh every tradition, including their own, by God's command and by love.

settings.what: The saying about uncleanness and its explanation
settings.to: The crowd (15:10–11), then the disciples privately (15:12–20)
settings.when: Right after the dispute with the Jerusalem visitors
settings.why: To teach where real impurity comes from: not from food passing through the body but from the heart, the source of evil plans and deeds. Peter calls the saying a parable, a riddle; Jesus explains it bluntly and lists sins against the second half of the Ten Commandments.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, Jewish believers who were learning to share a table with Gentiles, this teaching put moral holiness at the center of community life.
views: Read with Mark 7:19, the saying frees believers from the laws of clean and unclean food.
Read within Matthew (5:17–19; 15:20), it sets moral purity above ritual purity without cancelling the latter.

settings.what: The conversation with the Canaanite woman
settings.to: Each other, with the disciples listening
settings.when: In the borderlands of Tyre and Sidon, after Jesus has withdrawn from Galilee
settings.why: Her purpose is clear: to get help for her daughter. Jesus' purpose is debated. His silence and his harsh saying test her and state the order of his mission: Israel first. Her answer accepts the order but claims a share now, and he grants it.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, Jewish believers learning to welcome Gentiles, saw Israel's priority kept and Gentile faith honored, a step toward the mission to all nations (28:19).
views: Many interpreters, from Chrysostom on, hold that Jesus intended to help her and spoke to draw out and display her faith.
Some modern readers think the woman truly changed Jesus' mind, and that Matthew preserves a moment when his mission widened.
Others stress that the disciples wanted her sent away, and Jesus' answer exposes their attitude as much as tests hers.

settings.what: Jesus' compassion for the four thousand
settings.to: His disciples
settings.when: After three days of healing on a mountain by the lake
settings.why: To lead the disciples to share his concern for the hungry crowd and, once again, to see what God can do with little. Their question ("where would we find so many loaves?") shows they have not learned from the first feeding.
settings.readers: If the crowd was largely Gentile, as some think, Matthew's readers saw the bread offered first to Israel's children now shared with the nations.

traditions.q: How do Scripture and church tradition relate (15:3–9)?
views: Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition together form one deposit of God's word, interpreted by the Church's teaching office. Jesus condemns "human traditions" that oppose God's word, not the apostolic Tradition that hands on the gospel (Catechism 80–83).

Holy Tradition is the life of the Holy Spirit in the church, of which Scripture is the highest expression; the councils, the fathers and the liturgy belong to it. Customs that contradict this living Tradition are not true tradition.

Church traditions may be kept for good order, but none may be required as necessary for salvation or allowed to burden consciences. The Augsburg Confession builds this on Matthew 15: article 26, on the distinction of foods, cites 15:9 and 15:11, and article 28 applies the same principle to rules made by bishops.

Scripture alone is the rule of faith; nothing may be added to it "whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men" (Westminster Confession 1.6). Practices not commanded in Scripture should not be imposed in worship.

Scripture is the supreme standard by which "all human conduct, creeds, and religious opinions should be tried" (Baptist Faith and Message, art. 1). Traditions are judged by the Bible and hold no authority of their own.

traditions.q: Must Christians keep the Old Testament food laws (15:11)?
views: No. Jesus' teaching on food declared all foods clean (Catechism 582, citing Mark 7:18–21). The church sets its own days of fasting and abstinence as acts of penance, not as purity laws.
The biblical food laws do not bind Christians, but fasting from meat, dairy and other foods on many days of the year is an important discipline of the church, practiced for self-control and prayer.
No. The Augsburg Confession (art. 26) cites 15:11 and 15:9 against rules about foods imposed as necessary for grace, while allowing fasting as a free discipline.
The ceremonial laws, including food laws, pointed to Christ and are now ended under the new covenant (Westminster Confession 19.3).

The distinction between clean and unclean meats rests on health and was not abolished; Adventists abstain from unclean meats and encourage a vegetarian diet as stewardship of the body (Fundamental Belief 22). They read 15:11 as about hand-washing, not about which animals may be eaten.
Most evangelicals read 15:11 with Mark 7:19 and Acts 10 as freeing believers from food laws, while some Messianic Jewish congregations keep kosher as a matter of Jewish identity.

title: The Rock and the Cross
sum: Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven. Jesus answers that they can read the sky but not the signs of the times, and that the only sign they will get is the sign of Jonah. On the boat he warns the disciples against the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees; they think he means bread, until they understand that he means their teaching.

Near Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks who people say the Son of Man is, then who the disciples say he is. Simon Peter answers, "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God." Jesus calls him blessed, names him Peter, the rock on which he will build his church, and gives him the keys of the kingdom. From then on Jesus begins to teach that he must suffer, be killed and be raised on the third day. When Peter objects, Jesus calls him Satan and teaches that anyone who follows him must take up his cross; whoever loses his life for him will find it.
readings: Read as the turning point of the Gospel

The confession at Caesarea Philippi closes the first half of Jesus' ministry, in which the question was who he is. The words "From then on Jesus began" (16:21) open the second half, the road to Jerusalem and the cross. Peter is both the rock who confesses rightly and the stumbling block who cannot accept a suffering Messiah: a picture of every disciple.
Read as the founding of the church

Christians have long read 16:17–19 as Jesus' charter for the church. They agree that he promises to build a community that death will not overcome. They disagree, sometimes sharply, on whether the promise to Peter creates a lasting office passed on to his successors (see the card below).

views.H: Caesarea Philippi was a mostly Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon, rebuilt by Herod's son Philip around 2 BC. Crucifixion was a familiar Roman punishment in Galilee and Judea; Josephus records mass crucifixions after revolts. Most historians think Jesus foresaw that his mission in Jerusalem could end in his death, whatever they conclude about the detailed predictions.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 8:11–9:1 but adds the blessing of Peter (16:17–19), found in no other Gospel. Critical scholars debate whether these verses go back to Jesus, perhaps from a post-Easter setting (compare John 21:15–19), or were shaped in Matthew's community, where Peter was the leading apostle. Their Semitic style ("flesh and blood," "Bar-Jonah," "bind and loose") suggests an early, Aramaic-speaking source.
views.L: Peter moves from heaven-taught insight to Satan-inspired objection in a few verses. The word play runs on: Peter, named for the rock (petra), becomes a stone to trip over (skandalon, 16:23). "Behind me" links the rebuke of Peter with the call to follow (16:23–24). The chapter begins with leaders demanding a sign and ends with a promise that some will see the Son of Man in his kingdom.
views.J: The language of keys, binding and loosing comes straight from Jewish life: the palace steward of Isaiah 22 and the rabbinic authority to forbid and permit. Jewish readers will notice that Matthew gives Peter the role that the scribes and Pharisees claimed (23:2, 13). "The Messiah" in Jewish hope was a royal deliverer; the idea of a Messiah who must die was new and remains a central point of difference between Judaism and Christianity.
views.T: The words to Peter are written in giant letters around the dome of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. Catholics see in them the founding of the papacy; Orthodox and Protestant churches read them differently. The call to take up the cross shaped Christian spirituality from the martyrs to the monks and modern movements of discipleship.

deep.h: "On this rock": Peter, the keys and the church
deep.b:
Few verses have caused more disagreement among Christians than 16:18–19. The questions can be separated.

What is the rock? Four answers go back to the early church: Peter himself, Peter's confession of faith, Christ, and every believer who confesses as Peter did (see the note at 16:18). Many modern scholars, Protestant as well as Catholic, think the word play points most naturally to Peter, as the first to confess and the first leader of the apostles; they then add that this says nothing yet about successors.

Does Peter's role continue? Catholic teaching holds that Christ made Peter the visible head of the apostles and that this office continues in the bishop of Rome (First Vatican Council, 1870). The Orthodox churches honor Peter and grant Rome a primacy of honor among the ancient patriarchates, but hold that every bishop who teaches Peter's faith sits in his chair (Cyprian). Protestant churches deny that any bishop inherits a special authority from Peter, and generally see the keys given to the whole church through the preaching of the gospel (compare 18:18).

What do the keys and binding mean? The keys recall the royal steward of Isaiah 22:22; binding and loosing were Jewish terms for forbidding and permitting, and for excluding and readmitting. In 18:18 the same power is given to the disciples as a group. Whatever the answer to the papacy question, Matthew presents Peter as the first among the disciples, who is also the first to fail and be restored.

echoes: Deuteronomy 6:16; Jonah 1:17; Jonah 3:4–10; Exodus 12:15–20; Deuteronomy 8:2–3; Malachi 4:5; Psalm 42:2; Isaiah 51:1–2; Isaiah 28:16; Isaiah 22:20–22; Job 38:17; Isaiah 38:10; Hosea 6:2; Isaiah 8:14; Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12; Daniel 7:13–14; Mark 8:11–9:1; Luke 9:18–27; Luke 12:54–56; John 6:66–69; John 21:15–19

settings.what: The answer to the demand for a sign
settings.to: Pharisees and Sadducees who have come to test him
settings.when: After the second feeding, near Magadan (location unknown)
settings.why: To refuse a sign on demand and to expose the demand. People who can forecast weather from a red sky cannot see God's work in front of them. The only sign will be Jonah's: Jesus' death and resurrection, and a call to repent.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, facing the objection that Jesus gave no proof, are told that the decisive sign is the resurrection itself (12:40), and that no sign convinces those set against belief.

settings.what: The warning about yeast
settings.to: The disciples, on the boat, who have forgotten to bring bread
settings.when: Crossing the lake after the dispute about signs
settings.why: To warn them against the teaching and attitude of Israel's leaders, and to rebuke their worry about bread after they have seen two feedings. The disciples finally understand (16:12), as they do not in Mark.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers the warning concerned the rival teachers of their own day, and the rebuke reminded them that the Lord who fed the crowds would provide for them.

settings.what: Jesus' question, Peter's confession and Jesus' answer
settings.to: The disciples, gathered around Jesus
settings.when: Near Caesarea Philippi, at the northern edge of Jewish territory, toward the end of the Galilean ministry
settings.why: Jesus asks to bring the disciples to say who he is, and Peter's answer receives a blessing, a new name and a commission. The promise to build a church that death will not overcome looks beyond Jesus' own coming death. The order of silence keeps "Messiah" from being heard as a call to revolt.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, whose communities looked to Peter as the chief apostle, learned that their church rested on Jesus' promise and on the faith Peter confessed, and that its authority to bind and loose came from heaven.
views: Catholic readers see Jesus founding an office for Peter that continues in the bishop of Rome.
Orthodox readers hold that Peter was first among the apostles and that his succession lives in every bishop who keeps his faith; Rome once held a primacy of honor, not of jurisdiction.
Protestant readers see Peter as the first leader of the apostles, whose role as foundation was unique and passed to no office.
Others stress that Peter speaks for all the disciples and that the same authority is given to all of them in 18:18.

settings.what: The first prediction of the passion and the call to take up the cross
settings.to: The disciples (16:21–23), then all who would follow (16:24–28)
settings.when: "From then on": right after Peter's confession
settings.why: To teach what kind of Messiah he is: one who must suffer, die and be raised. Peter's protest shows the human idea of a Messiah; Jesus' rebuke and teaching show God's way, in which the disciple follows the same road.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, some of whom faced loss and persecution, heard that following Jesus means carrying a cross, and that losing life for him is the way to find it.

traditions.q: Did Jesus make Peter and his successors the head of the church (16:18–19)?
views: Yes. Christ made Peter head of the apostles and the visible foundation of the church's unity, and this primacy continues in the bishop of Rome. The pope holds "full and supreme power of jurisdiction over the whole church," which is "ordinary and immediate" (Pastor Aeternus 3). He "has full, supreme and universal power over the Church" and "is always free to exercise this power" (Lumen Gentium 22; Catechism 882). When he defines a doctrine of faith or morals ex cathedra, he teaches infallibly (Pastor Aeternus 4). The bishops govern the whole church as a college only together with him, and recent popes describe the office as a service of unity (Ut Unum Sint 94–96).

Peter was first among the apostles, and his succession lives in every bishop who keeps his faith. Cyprian taught that the other apostles were what Peter was and that the episcopate is one (On the Unity of the Church 4–5, received text). Rome once held a primacy of honor among the patriarchates, not jurisdiction over the whole church, and no bishop rules the church apart from the councils. At Ravenna (2007) Catholic and Orthodox theologians agreed that some primacy exists at the universal level, without agreeing what it involves; the Moscow Patriarchate did not sign and later rejected a universal primacy of jurisdiction (2013).

The rock is the faith Peter confessed, and the keys belong to the whole church, not to one person. The pope holds no authority over other bishops by divine right (Melanchthon, Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope, 1537; Smalcald Articles II.4). Many Protestant scholars today, following the Lutheran Oscar Cullmann, agree that the rock is Peter himself, but as the unrepeatable foundation apostle, with no successor.
Calvin held that Christ alone is the foundation and that what was given to Peter was given equally to all the apostles; he rejected any succession of Peter's authority in Rome (Institutes 4.6.1–7).

"The Bishop of Rome hath no jurisdiction in this Realm of England" (Article 37). In recent dialogue, Anglican and Catholic theologians have explored whether a universal primacy could serve unity (ARCIC, The Gift of Authority, 1999), without agreement on its basis.

No. "The Lord Jesus Christ is the Head of the church," and "neither can the Pope of Rome in any sense be head thereof" (London Confession 1689, 26.4). The Baptist Faith and Message (art. 6) describes each church as an autonomous local congregation under the lordship of Christ and does not discuss Peter. Many Baptist interpreters read the rock as Peter's confession of Christ, or as Peter the first confessor, with no successor.

title: Glory on the Mountain, Need Below
sum: Six days later Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, and is transformed before them: his face shines like the sun and his clothes become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear and talk with him. Peter offers to build three booths, but a bright cloud covers them and a voice says, "This is my dearly loved Son; in him I take delight. Listen to him!" The disciples fall down in fear, and Jesus tells them to get up. On the way down he tells them that Elijah has already come, meaning John the Baptist.

Below the mountain a father kneels before Jesus: the disciples could not heal his son, who suffers seizures. Jesus rebukes the faithless generation, drives out the demon, and tells the disciples that faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains. In Galilee he predicts his death and resurrection a second time. At Capernaum the collectors of the Temple tax ask whether Jesus pays it. Jesus says that kings' sons are free, but so as not to give offense, he sends Peter to find a coin in a fish's mouth and pay for both of them.
readings: Read as an event

The church has read the transfiguration as something the three disciples saw, a glimpse of the glory that belonged to Jesus and would be revealed at the resurrection. 2 Peter 1:16–18 appeals to it as eyewitness testimony.
Read as a vision shaped by Scripture

Many scholars note how closely the scene follows Moses on Sinai (six days, a mountain, three companions, a cloud, a voice, a shining face) and Matthew's own word "vision" (17:9). They read it as an experience of the disciples, told in the language of Exodus, to show Jesus as the prophet like Moses whom Israel must hear.

views.H: The Gospels do not name the mountain. Tabor, the traditional site, is low and may have had a settlement on top; Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, is much higher. The half-shekel Temple tax is well attested before AD 70; after the Temple's fall, Rome collected the same sum from all Jews for the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, a tax still in force when Matthew wrote.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 9:2–32 but adds the disciples' fear and Jesus' touch (17:6–7), shortens the healing story, and adds the saying on mustard-seed faith (17:20; compare Luke 17:6). The Temple tax story (17:24–27) is found only in Matthew. Many critical scholars think it addressed whether Matthew's Jewish-Christian readers should pay the Jewish tax, either to the Temple or, later, to Rome.
views.L: The chapter moves from the mountain to the valley, from glory to failure, as Moses came down from Sinai to the golden calf. Two words to Peter frame it: the Father's "Listen to him" and Jesus' "Simon, how does it seem to you?" (17:25). The voice calls Jesus "Son"; the tax story calls his followers "sons" who go free.
views.J: Moses and Elijah are the two great figures of Israel's covenant and of its hopes for the end. Malachi's promise of Elijah's return before the day of the LORD is still read on the Sabbath before Passover. The Temple tax was paid gladly by most Jews as a sign of belonging; Jesus' payment, "so that we do not trip them up," shows him honoring that practice.
views.T: The feast of the Transfiguration (6 August) is one of the great feasts in the Orthodox calendar, where it is central to the teaching on theosis, the believer's sharing in God's glory. Icons show Christ in a mandorla of light, with the three disciples thrown to the ground. In the West the scene was often read as a preview of the resurrection body.

deep.b:
Matthew's account echoes Exodus closely. At Sinai the cloud covered the mountain for six days, and on the seventh God called Moses (Exodus 24:16). Moses took three named companions (Exodus 24:1, 9). When he came down, his face shone (Exodus 34:29–35). God's glory filled the tent in a cloud (Exodus 40:34–35). And Moses had promised a prophet like himself: "You must listen to him" (Deuteronomy 18:15).

Matthew sharpens these echoes. Only he says Jesus' face "blazed like the sun," and only he has the disciples fall on their faces in fear and Jesus come and touch them. The point is not that Jesus is simply a new Moses: Moses himself is present, and the voice singles out the Son. Moses reflected glory; Jesus shines with it. The Law and the Prophets stand with him, and then the disciples see "nobody... except Jesus, alone" (17:8).

Coming right after the first prediction of the passion, the vision assures the disciples that the road to the cross is the road of God's beloved Son, and it points ahead to the resurrection, which is why they must keep silent until then (17:9).

echoes: Exodus 24:1–18; Exodus 34:29–35; Exodus 40:34–35; Deuteronomy 18:15; Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 42:1; Genesis 22:2; Daniel 12:3; Leviticus 23:42–43; Malachi 4:4–6; 1 Kings 19:8–18; 2 Kings 2:11; Deuteronomy 32:5; Numbers 14:27; Exodus 30:11–16; Mark 9:2–32; Luke 9:28–45; 2 Peter 1:16–18

settings.what: The voice from the cloud
settings.by: A voice from the bright cloud (God, who calls Jesus "my Son")
settings.to: Peter, James and John, and through them all the disciples
settings.when: While Peter is still speaking about the booths, on the mountain
settings.why: To confirm who Jesus is, in the same words as at his baptism, and to add the command "Listen to him!": listen to his teaching, including his hard words about the cross (16:21–28). The voice sets the Son above Moses and Elijah.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, who had the Law and the Prophets and also Jesus' teaching, were told whom to listen to first: the Son, whose words fulfill the Law and the Prophets (5:17).

settings.what: The command to silence and the question about Elijah
settings.to: Each other, on the way down the mountain
settings.when: Right after the vision
settings.why: To keep the vision secret until the resurrection, and to answer the scribes' objection that Elijah must come before the Messiah. Jesus answers that Elijah came in John the Baptist and was rejected, and that the Son of Man will suffer the same way.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, who heard Jewish neighbors ask "Where was Elijah?", received an answer: Elijah came in John.

settings.what: The rebuke and the saying about faith
settings.to: The crowd and the father (17:17), then the disciples alone (17:20)
settings.when: At the foot of the mountain, after the disciples failed to heal the boy
settings.why: To grieve over the unbelief around him, to heal the boy, and to teach the disciples that their failure came from small faith. Even faith as small as a mustard seed, trusting God and not itself, can do the impossible.
settings.readers: Matthew's church, which also failed at times, learned that its power came from trust in God, not from technique or status.
views: Many readers take Jesus to mean that the disciples' faith was too weak to act on.
Others note that Matthew's word (oligopistia) describes faith that doubts (14:31), not faith that is too little in amount, since even mustard-seed faith suffices.

settings.what: The second prediction of the passion
settings.to: The disciples, as they gather in Galilee
settings.when: Before leaving Galilee for Jerusalem
settings.why: To prepare them again for his death and resurrection, now adding that he will be "handed over." This time they understand enough to be deeply grieved.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers saw that Jesus went to his death knowingly, as God's plan, not as a victim of chance.

settings.what: The question about the Temple tax and Jesus' answer
settings.by: The tax collectors, Peter and Jesus
settings.to: Peter at Capernaum, then Peter in the house
settings.when: On arrival in Capernaum, probably near the time the tax was collected in spring
settings.why: To settle whether Jesus pays the yearly half-shekel. Jesus argues that God's sons are free from a tax for their Father's house, yet pays to avoid giving offense. Freedom gives way to love.
settings.readers: Before AD 70 the tax supported the Temple; afterward Rome took it from all Jews for a pagan temple. Either way, Matthew's Jewish-Christian readers learned to pay rather than cause offense, while knowing they were free.
views: Most scholars think the story first concerned the tax for the Jerusalem Temple, based on Exodus 30:11–16.
Some think Matthew's readers would also have applied it to the tax Rome imposed after AD 70.

title: Life Together in the Church
sum: The disciples ask who ranks highest in the kingdom of heaven. Jesus places a child among them: unless they turn and become like children, they will not even enter. Whoever welcomes such a child welcomes him, and whoever trips up one of these little ones would be better off drowned. Cut off whatever trips you up; do not look down on the little ones, whose angels see the Father's face. Like a shepherd seeking one stray sheep, the Father does not want even one of them lost.

If a brother sins, correct him privately; if he will not listen, take one or two others; then tell the church; if he still refuses, treat him as an outsider. What the disciples bind and loose on earth stands in heaven, and where two or three gather in Jesus' name, he is with them. Peter asks if he should forgive seven times; Jesus answers, seventy-seven times. He tells of a slave forgiven a vast debt who refused to forgive a fellow slave a small one, and was handed over to the torturers. So the Father will do to anyone who does not forgive from the heart.
readings: Read as rules for the church

The fourth of Matthew's five discourses is the nearest thing in the Gospels to a church order. It covers rank, care for the weak, correcting members, discipline, prayer and forgiveness. Churches have drawn from it their practices of discipline and excommunication.
Read as a call to humility and mercy

The discourse is framed by a child (18:2) and a parable about forgiveness (18:23–35). Its rules sit inside that frame: discipline is for winning back the brother, and authority belongs to those who make themselves low. Read this way, the chapter warns against harsh discipline as much as it commands it.

views.H: Communities of Jesus' followers met in houses, and needed ways to settle disputes, as other Jewish groups did. The Dead Sea Scrolls show a strikingly similar procedure of rebuke before witnesses and before the assembly. The sums in the parable fit the world of royal finance: a talent was about 6,000 denarii, and Herod Antipas's whole yearly income was about 200 talents.
views.C: Matthew builds the discourse from Mark 9:33–50, sayings shared with Luke (Luke 15:4–7; Luke 17:1–4) and his own material (18:15–20, 23–35). Many scholars think 18:15–20 reflects the life of Matthew's own community, since it speaks of "the church" as an existing body. Others note that Jesus could well have given rules to the renewed Israel he was gathering.
views.L: The chapter is held together by repeated words: "little ones" (18:6, 10, 14), "brother" (18:15, 21, 35), "trip up" (18:6–9), and the numbers one, two, three, seven, ninety-nine and ten thousand. It moves from the question of greatness to the answer of forgiveness, and from the lost sheep sought by the Father to the brother won back by the disciple.
views.J: Jesus' teaching draws on Leviticus 19:17–18 (rebuke your neighbor, love your neighbor) and Deuteronomy 19:15 (two or three witnesses). The saying about two or three gathered in his name closely parallels a Jewish saying about the Divine Presence among those who study Torah. Jewish teaching on forgiveness also requires the wrongdoer to seek reconciliation; Matthew puts the first step on the one who was wronged (18:15).
views.T: Churches have built very different practices on this chapter: the sacrament of penance and excommunication (Catholic and Orthodox), church courts and discipline (Reformed), the ban and shunning (Anabaptist and Amish), and congregational discipline (Baptist). The verse about angels became the main basis for belief in guardian angels, honored in a Catholic feast on 2 October.

deep.h: The church discourse and church discipline
deep.b:
Matthew 18:15–17 sets out three steps: speak to the brother alone, then with one or two witnesses, then before the church; if he refuses even the church, treat him "as the Gentile and the tax collector." Paul's letters show similar practices: the Corinthians must remove a man living in open sin (1 Corinthians 5), and the Thessalonians must keep apart from the disobedient, yet warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

The setting shapes the rules. Before them comes the parable of the straying sheep (18:12–14); after them comes the command to forgive without limit (18:21–35). The first aim is to "win your brother back" (18:15). Many interpreters therefore read the final step as a last call to repentance, not a final judgment. Others stress that a church that never acts against public sin fails both the sinner and the little ones he may harm (18:6).

Christian practices differ widely (see the cards below), but nearly all claim this passage, and nearly all agree on the order: privately first, publicly only as a last resort.

echoes: Leviticus 19:17–18; Deuteronomy 19:15; Deuteronomy 17:6; Ezekiel 34:4–16; Psalm 91:11; Esther 1:14; Genesis 4:24; 2 Kings 4:1; Mark 9:33–50; Luke 9:46–48; Luke 15:3–7; Luke 17:1–4; John 20:22–23; 1 Corinthians 5:1–13; 2 Thessalonians 3:14–15

settings.what: The church discourse, the fourth of Matthew's five discourses
settings.to: The disciples, who have asked who ranks highest (18:1); Peter asks a question part way through (18:21)
settings.when: At Capernaum, shortly before Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea (19:1)
settings.why: To shape the life of the community he is gathering: humble rather than rank-seeking, protective of the weak, ready to correct and quick to forgive.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, a church living with internal disputes and failures, received practical instructions for handling sin and a reminder that all of it must be done as people who have been forgiven a vast debt.

settings.what: The child in the middle, and the warning about snares
settings.to: The disciples
settings.when: In answer to their question about rank
settings.why: To overturn their question: the way into the kingdom is to become low like a child; welcoming the lowly is welcoming Jesus; and causing a weak believer to fall is so serious that drastic measures are better.
settings.readers: In Matthew's church, "little ones" were humble and vulnerable believers, and the warning fell on anyone, especially leaders, whose conduct might destroy their faith.

settings.what: The parable of the straying sheep
settings.to: The disciples (in Luke 15:3–7, Pharisees and scribes)
settings.when: In the discourse, between the warning about snares and the rules for correcting a brother
settings.why: To show the Father's will that not one of the little ones be lost, and so the disciples' duty to seek out those who stray.
settings.readers: For Matthew's church the straying sheep was a fellow believer drifting away; the parable sets the tone for the discipline that follows.
views: In Matthew the parable is about care for straying church members.
In Luke it defends Jesus' welcome of sinners against his critics. Many scholars think Jesus told it in some such setting, and each Gospel applied it to its readers.

settings.what: The rule for correcting a brother
settings.to: The disciples ("you" plural in 18:18–20)
settings.when: In the discourse
settings.why: To set out a fair, step-by-step way to deal with sin within the community, aimed at winning the brother back, and to assure the disciples that God stands behind decisions made together in Jesus' name.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers had a real "church" to tell; the steps protected both the accused, by witnesses, and the community, by a final decision.

settings.what: Peter's question about forgiveness
settings.to: Each other, before the disciples
settings.when: After the teaching on correcting a brother
settings.why: Peter wants a limit, and offers a generous one. Jesus removes the limit with Lamech's number, seventy-seven.
settings.readers: For a church that had to correct sinners, this reminded them that correction never ends forgiveness.

settings.what: The parable of the unforgiving slave
settings.to: Peter and the disciples
settings.when: Ending the discourse
settings.why: To show why forgiveness must be without limit: those who have been forgiven an unpayable debt by God cannot refuse to forgive small debts to one another. The ending warns that refusing to forgive means losing God's forgiveness.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers prayed "forgive us the debts we owe, just as we ourselves have forgiven the people who owe us" (6:12); the parable dramatizes that prayer.

traditions.q: How should a church discipline a member who will not repent (18:15–17)?
views: Grave and public sins can bring excommunication, which bars a person from the sacraments until he repents; it is meant as a medicine, to lead to conversion, and is lifted by absolution (Code of Canon Law 1331, 1358).
Bishops and priests may bar a person from Communion for a time as a penance; the aim is healing, and discipline is applied with oikonomia, pastoral flexibility for the person's good.
The church uses the "office of the keys": unrepentant open sinners are refused the Lord's Supper until they repent, but this is done by the word, not by force (Smalcald Articles III.9).

Church discipline is one of the marks of a true church (Belgic Confession 29, 32). Elders admonish, suspend from the Lord's Supper and, as a last step, excommunicate, for the honor of Christ and the good of the sinner (Westminster Confession 30).

The ban follows the steps of 18:15–17 and is practiced before the Lord's Supper (Schleitheim, art. 2). Some groups, such as the Amish, also practice shunning, avoiding social contact with a banned member, following the Dordrecht Confession (art. 16–17); Mennonites today mostly practice discipline without shunning.

Discipline belongs to the whole congregation, which follows the steps of 18:15–17 and may remove an unrepentant member from membership (London Confession 1689, ch. 26.12). Practice varies widely among Baptist churches today.

traditions.q: What is the authority to bind and loose, and to forgive sins (16:19; 18:18)?
views: Christ gave the apostles and their successors, the bishops, with priests as their helpers, the power to forgive sins in his name in the sacrament of penance, and the power to admit to or exclude from communion (Catechism 553, 1444–1445).
The power to bind and loose belongs to the church and is exercised by bishops and priests in confession, where the priest acts as a witness and the forgiveness comes from Christ.

The office of the keys is the power Christ gave his church to forgive the sins of the repentant and to retain the sins of the unrepentant; private confession and absolution are retained (Augsburg Confession 25, 28; the section on the Office of the Keys added to Luther's Small Catechism).
The keys are the preaching of the gospel and church discipline: by them the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and shut against unbelievers (Heidelberg Catechism Q83–85).

Christ has given each local church all the power it needs for worship and discipline, including receiving and excluding members; the congregation exercises it together with its elders (London Confession 1689, 26.7–12).

traditions.q: Does every person have a guardian angel (18:10)?
views: Yes. "From its beginning until death, human life is surrounded by their watchful care and intercession. Beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd" (Catechism 336, quoting Basil). A feast of the Guardian Angels is kept on 2 October.
Yes. Each Christian receives a guardian angel at baptism, and prayers to the guardian angel are part of daily Orthodox prayer.
Calvin judged it uncertain whether each believer has one particular angel; it is enough to know that all the angels care for our salvation (Institutes 1.14.7).
Most affirm that God sends angels to protect believers (Psalm 91:11; Hebrews 1:14), but many hold that Scripture does not teach that each person has one assigned angel.
